name: Spinlock from The Art of Writing Efficient Programs
listed_description: Chapter 18 only points to the author's other book for spinlocks that guard short critical sections and are more efficient than std::mutex; no code or numbers appear in this book.
claim_text: There are much more efficient locks than std::mutex (for example, spinlocks for guarding short computations)
book_benchmark: Nothing measured in this book. The claim is a pointer to the author's other book, whose companion repository (MIT license) could not be confirmed to hold spinlock code from its top-level directory listing.
found_in: book: Hands-On Design Patterns with C++, 2nd ed. (2023), ch. 18, Patterns for Concurrency, Synchronization patterns, Mutex and locking patterns (closing paragraph)

name: Thread-specific cache-line-aligned counters
listed_description: Each thread increments its own counter, padded to a 64-byte cache line to avoid false sharing, and the counters are summed after join; presented as better than a mutex-guarded shared count.
book_benchmark: No timing in the book. Examples 5 to 8 of chapter 18 contrast a mutex-guarded shared counter with a per-thread local count, a per-thread variable aligned to 64 bytes, and a once-per-thread merge. The code is in the Chapter18 directory of the companion repository.
found_in: book: Hands-On Design Patterns with C++, 2nd ed. (2023), ch. 18, Synchronization patterns, No sharing is the best sharing

name: Relaxed atomic counter and atomic index
listed_description: std::atomic fetch_add with relaxed ordering used as a shared counter or as an array index handed to producer threads, instead of a mutex around a simple increment.
claim_text: using a mutex to protect a simple increment of an integer is highly inefficient
book_benchmark: No timing in the book. Examples 15 and 16 of chapter 18 show the atomic counter and the atomic index; the baseline is a mutex-protected increment. Code is in the Chapter18 directory of the companion repository.
found_in: book: Hands-On Design Patterns with C++, 2nd ed. (2023), ch. 18, Synchronization patterns, Lock-free synchronization patterns

name: std::atomic_flag wait/notify (C++20)
listed_description: C++20 atomic_flag wait() with notify_one() or notify_all() as a blocking wait for another thread, compared in the text with an explicit busy-polling loop on the flag.
claim_text: its implementation is almost certainly more efficient than our simple polling loop
book_benchmark: No timing in the book. Chapter 18 Examples 12 and 13 contrast the busy-poll loop with the wait/notify version; the book calls efficiency out of scope.
found_in: book: Hands-On Design Patterns with C++, 2nd ed. (2023), ch. 18, Synchronization patterns, Waiting patterns
